Write a custom immutable class, and override equals/hashCode
Write a custom checked exception
Sort custom objects with Comparable and Comparator (several fields, nulls)

Comparable defines one natural order inside the class (compareTo). Comparator defines any number of external orders. Use Integer.compare rather than a - b, because subtraction can overflow. Keep compareTo consistent with equals if the objects go into a TreeSet or TreeMap, because those use compareTo to decide duplicates. Sorting is O(n log n) and List.sort is stable (TimSort).
Remove elements from a list while iterating (avoid ConcurrentModificationException)

The for-each loop uses an iterator that is fail-fast: it checks the list's modCount and throws if the list was changed structurally by anything other than the iterator itself. Use Iterator.remove() or removeIf. Concurrent collections such as CopyOnWriteArrayList and ConcurrentHashMap have fail-safe (weakly consistent) iterators that never throw. Note that List.of(...) is immutable, so it throws UnsupportedOperationException on any removal.
Implement your own HashMap (put, get, chaining, resize)

The key ideas: hashCode() picks the bucket, equals() finds the key inside the bucket, and the table doubles when size exceeds capacity × load factor (0.75). That is why a key that changes its hashCode after insertion gets "lost". get/put are O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case for one long chain. The real java.util.HashMap turns a bucket into a red-black tree once it holds 8 or more entries (and the table has at least 64 buckets), which makes the worst case O(log n).
Generic methods and classes: max of a list, and a Pair<A, B>

Generics give compile-time type safety and remove casts. They are implemented by type erasure, so at runtime List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class: you can't do new T(), new T[n] or instanceof List<String>. Use ? extends T when you only read from a collection and ? super T when you only write to it.
Read a file and count lines, words and characters (try-with-resources)

Any class that implements AutoCloseable can be used in try-with-resources; resources are closed in reverse order, even if an exception is thrown, and an exception from close() is attached as a suppressed exception instead of hiding the original. Files.lines is lazy, so it must itself be closed. Time O(n), memory O(1) for the streaming versions.
Java 21: records, sealed interfaces and pattern-matching switch (area of shapes)

A record is a final, immutable data carrier with generated constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString. A sealed interface lists every allowed subtype, so the compiler can check that a switch covers all cases; if someone adds a new shape, every switch without a default stops compiling, which is exactly what you want. Record patterns (deconstruction) and when guards are final in Java 21.
Pangram check, and count the words in a sentence

The pangram check is O(n) time and O(1) space (a fixed 26-slot array; a 26-bit int mask also works). For word counting, split on the regex \s+ after stripping, otherwise leading spaces produce an empty first token and the count is off by one.
String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer: which do you use to build or reverse a string?

| String | StringBuilder | StringBuffer
Mutable | No | Yes | Yes
Thread-safe | Yes (immutable) | No | Yes (synchronized methods)
+= in a loop | New object each time, O(n²) total | append is amortised O(1) | Same, plus lock cost
Has reverse() | No | Yes | Yes
Use for | Keys, constants, values you pass around | Building strings in one method | Legacy code only
Rule of thumb: StringBuilder for anything built in a loop; String everywhere else. A single a + b + c expression is fine, the compiler optimises it; the problem is concatenation inside a loop.
int vs long vs BigInteger: when does factorial (or Fibonacci) overflow?

| int | long | BigInteger
Max value | 2,147,483,647 (about 2.1 × 10⁹) | about 9.2 × 10¹⁸ | Limited only by memory
Largest factorial that fits | 12! | 20! | Any
Largest Fibonacci term that fits | F(46) | F(92) | Any
On overflow | Wraps silently to a wrong value | Wraps silently | Never overflows
Speed | Fastest | Fast | Much slower, creates objects
Interview tip: mention overflow before the interviewer does. Use Math.multiplyExact / Math.addExact if you want an ArithmeticException instead of a silent wrong answer.
Recursion vs iteration vs memoization (Fibonacci as the example)

| Plain recursion | Recursion + memo | Iteration (two variables)
Time for fib(n) | O(2ⁿ) (about O(1.6ⁿ)) | O(n) | O(n)
Extra space | O(n) call stack | O(n) stack + O(n) cache | O(1)
StackOverflowError risk | Yes, for deep n | Yes, for deep n | No
Readability | Matches the formula | Formula + a map | Slightly more bookkeeping
Rule of thumb: write the recursive version to show the idea, then point out the repeated work and convert to memo or a loop. Java has no tail-call optimisation, so deep recursion always costs stack frames.
== vs equals() vs compareTo() for Strings and Integers

| == | equals() | compareTo()
Compares | References (same object?) | Content | Order: negative, 0 or positive
"ab" == "ab" (literals) | true (string pool) | true | 0
new String("ab") == "ab" | false | true | 0
Integer 127 vs 127 | true (cached -128..127) | true | 0
Integer 128 vs 128 | false (by default) | true | 0
Rule of thumb: use == only for primitives and enums. For objects use equals (or Objects.equals(a, b) when either may be null) and compareTo when you need ordering.
HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap for counting characters

| HashMap | LinkedHashMap | TreeMap
Iteration order | Not defined | Insertion order | Sorted by key
get / put | O(1) average | O(1) average | O(log n)
Null key | One allowed | One allowed | No (with natural ordering)
Best for | Just the counts | "First non-repeating character" | Output sorted a→z
Interview tip: for lowercase letters only, an int[26] beats every map. Pick the map by the order the output needs.
